prompt: Match each kind of survey to what it shows.
hint: Modelled, listened to, or connected.

pairs.right: A design and a budget before anything is bought
The signal, noise and channels on the air
The throughput and roams a connected user gets

right_distractors: Non-Wi-Fi energy from a microwave oven

prompt: A predictive design for a clinic was built with every interior wall entered as plasterboard. Some are concrete. What happens to the design?
hint: The model is only as good as its inputs.

choices.text: Nothing, since the software corrects walls from the floor plan
choices.why: A floor plan shows where a wall is, not what it is made of.

choices.text: Its cells behind those walls are metres too large
choices.why: Right. Concrete costs far more than plasterboard, so the real cell edges come sooner.

choices.text: It overestimates the noise floor
choices.why: Wall materials change the signal, not the noise.

choices.text: It chooses the wrong band for the clients
choices.why: The band is a requirement, not an output of the wall model.

prompt: A warehouse survey was walked with a laptop. The staff use handheld scanners with small antennas. What is wrong with the survey?
hint: Which device decides the design?

choices.text: Laptops cannot measure 5 GHz
choices.why: They measure it fine; the question is how their reading compares with the scanners'.

choices.text: The survey should have been predictive
choices.why: A prediction would carry the same assumption about the client, and less evidence.

choices.text: Scanners are not Wi-Fi clients
choices.why: They are, and the weakest ones on this network.

choices.text: It measured a better radio than the weakest client's
choices.why: Right. The scanners hear less and are heard less, so the cells they can use are smaller than the map.

prompt: What is an AP on a stick for?
hint: A real AP, a temporary place.

choices.text: Replacing a failed AP until a new one arrives
choices.why: That is a spare, not a survey tool.

choices.text: Measuring where a planned AP's cell really ends
choices.why: Right. It settles a difficult area before the cabling is paid for.

choices.text: Finding non-Wi-Fi interference
choices.why: That takes a spectrum analyser; an AP only sees a busy channel.

choices.text: Extra coverage at an event
choices.why: The tripod places it where the design puts it, to measure, not to serve.

prompt: fspl.py gave 72.2 dB at 40 m on 2437 MHz. What is the free-space loss at 80 m on the same channel, in dB?
hint: Doubling the distance.

prompt: In free space, why does a 5 GHz signal arrive 7.1 dB weaker than a 2.4 GHz one over the same distance?
hint: There are no walls in free space.

choices.text: The air absorbs higher frequencies more
choices.why: Over tens of metres the air absorbs almost nothing at either frequency.

choices.text: 5 GHz APs are allowed less transmit power
choices.why: The formula is a loss between two points; the transmit power is not in it.

choices.text: A shorter wave's antenna collects less
choices.why: Right. Its effective area shrinks with the wavelength, so it catches less of the same wave.

choices.text: 5 GHz channels are wider, spreading the power
choices.why: Channel width is not in the free-space formula; the table used the same formula for all three.

prompt: Indoors, the lesson's heat map used a loss of 35 dB per tenfold of distance. How many dB is that per doubling, to one decimal place?
A concrete wall costs 20 dB. What share of the signal's power gets through it?
hint: Every 10 dB is a factor of ten.

choices.text: A fifth
choices.why: That would be about 7 dB.

choices.text: A twentieth
choices.why: Decibels are logarithmic: 20 dB is not a factor of 20.

choices.text: A thousandth
choices.why: That is 30 dB, three factors of ten.

choices.text: A hundredth
choices.why: Right. Two factors of ten.

prompt: A survey reads a signal of −64 dBm on a noise floor of −91 dBm. What is the SNR, in dB?
hint: Signal minus noise.

prompt: Why do voice designs aim for −67 dBm at the cell edge rather than just above the point where a phone stops working?
hint: Two reasons: margin and roaming.

choices.text: Margin, and an early roam
choices.why: Right. A hand, a smaller antenna and fading take a few dB, and the phone should find the next AP before the call suffers.

choices.text: The 802.11 standard sets it for voice
choices.why: It comes from vendors' guides and practice, not from 802.11.

choices.text: Phones refuse to associate below −67 dBm
choices.why: Clients associate far below that; roaming thresholds sit around −70 to −75.

choices.text: Voice codecs need exactly that signal level
choices.why: A codec cares about loss and delay; the signal level matters through them.

prompt: A survey shows −66 dBm at the far end of a corridor, yet phones there drop calls, and the AP's logs show their frames arriving weak and retried. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: The survey measured one direction.

choices.text: The survey adapter was faulty
choices.why: Nothing suggests that; the AP's own logs point at the other direction.

choices.text: The AP's power is too low for the corridor
choices.why: The phones hear the AP well; raising its power widens the imbalance.

choices.text: The phones' weaker uplink fails first
choices.why: Right. The survey measured the AP's signal; the phones' weaker transmitters are the limit here.

choices.text: −66 dBm is below the voice target
choices.why: It is 1 dB above −67.

prompt: Two spots both read −60 dBm. At one, a microwave oven has raised the noise floor to −75 dBm. What differs between them?
hint: What decides the data rate?

choices.text: Nothing, since the signal is the same
choices.why: Same signal, different noise: the SNR is what the client works from.

choices.text: Their SNR, and so the data rate
choices.why: Right. −60 minus −75 is 15 dB, well below the 25 dB a voice design asks for.

choices.text: The channel the AP picks
choices.why: The channel is the AP's configuration; the question is about the link at that spot.

choices.text: The roaming threshold of the client
choices.why: That threshold is a signal level, and the signal is identical.

prompt: A hotel floor has twelve APs at full power, and its primary-signal heat map is the strongest colour from wall to wall. Guests complain the Wi-Fi is slow. Which view of the survey would show the problem?
hint: Too much signal looks like good coverage.

choices.text: Secondary signal
choices.why: Secondary coverage would be strong too; it answers whether roaming has somewhere to go.

choices.text: Channel overlap
choices.why: Right. Twelve loud APs on a few channels hear each other and take turns on the air.

choices.text: Primary signal at a lower threshold
choices.why: Recolouring the same values still shows only the strongest AP.

choices.text: The walked path
choices.why: The path shows where was measured, not why it is slow.

prompt: In the lesson's heat map, what made the corner behind the lift core fall below −75 dBm?
hint: It is not far from B.

choices.text: Its distance from every AP
choices.why: B is not far away; the corner is in the core's shadow.

choices.text: Interference from the lift motor
choices.why: The model has no interference in it; it is signal only.

choices.text: 15 dB of concrete in the way
choices.why: Right. A dead spot made by a wall, not by distance.

choices.text: B and C sharing a channel
choices.why: Channels are not in this model, and sharing one does not lower the signal.

prompt: Which of these does a primary-signal heat map NOT show? Choose all that apply.
hint: It shows one AP per spot: the strongest.

choices.text: Whether a second AP is there to roam to
choices.why: Right. That is the secondary view.

choices.text: Where the strongest signal falls below −75 dBm
choices.why: That is exactly what it shows.

choices.text: The noise at each spot
choices.why: Right. Noise needs the SNR view.

choices.text: How many APs share each channel
choices.why: Right. That is the channel-overlap view.

choices.text: Which spots were measured and which were interpolated
choices.why: Right. The walked path has to be drawn with it.

prompt: A survey's heat map shows a meeting room in the strongest colour, but the walked path never entered it. What does the colour there mean?
hint: Where does colour come from between measured points?

choices.text: The room was measured from the corridor
choices.why: The corridor was measured; the room behind its wall was not.

choices.text: The room is covered, since interpolation is conservative
choices.why: Interpolation smooths between points and knows nothing about the wall it paints across.

choices.text: A guess painted in by the software
choices.why: Right. A room nobody entered is not covered, whatever colour it has.

choices.text: The AP inside the room was switched off
choices.why: Nothing says there is an AP in the room; the colour is interpolation.

prompt: Why are the exceptions the most useful page of a survey document?
hint: A weak stairwell with and without a line about it.

choices.text: They list the APs to buy
choices.why: That is the bill of materials.

choices.text: They record accepted gaps, and why
choices.why: Right. An accepted gap is a decision; an unrecorded one is a fault waiting for a ticket.

choices.text: They show the strongest signal on the floor
choices.why: The heat maps do that; the exceptions record where the design fell short.

choices.text: They prove the survey adapter was calibrated
choices.why: The adapter and its offset have their own part.

prompt: After installation, which check finds a voice problem that no heat map can show?
hint: A heat map is a still picture.

choices.text: A second passive survey of the whole floor
choices.why: Passive surveys draw signal maps too; they do not follow a call.

choices.text: A spectrum analysis around the lift shaft
choices.why: That finds interference, and only near the lift.

choices.text: The channel-overlap view
choices.why: Useful, and still a map of a moment rather than a moving call.

choices.text: A call walked along the busiest route
choices.why: Right. It shows every roam, and where a call drops.

prompt: Validation finds a ward at −72 dBm where the target was −67. Why is turning that AP's power up the wrong fix?
hint: Which direction does more power help?

choices.text: Enterprise APs are shipped at their maximum power already
choices.why: Enterprise APs are rarely at maximum; the objection is what the extra power does.

choices.text: The survey adapter would stop reading it
choices.why: More power reads as more signal; the adapter is not the problem.

choices.text: Only the downlink improves, and overlap grows
choices.why: Right. The phones still answer at their own power, and more APs now hear each other.

choices.text: Higher power breaks 802.11r
choices.why: Fast roaming does not depend on transmit power.

prompt: Put the steps of a Wi-Fi design and survey in order.
hint: Measure against something written first.
items: Write down the requirements and the weakest client
Check the doubtful walls on site with an AP on a stick
Survey again, passive and active, against the requirements
trap: Validation comes after installation and is judged against the requirements written at the start.

prompt: An AP radiates 18 dBm at 5500 MHz. fspl.py gives 67.3 dB of free-space loss at 10 m. A client 10 m away is behind one concrete wall costing 15 dB. What signal does it receive, in dBm?
hint: Radiated, minus the path, minus the wall.

prompt: A warehouse passed its validation survey in March. In November, with the racks full for the holidays, scanners drop out in the far aisles. What is the right response?
hint: What changed is the building, not the network.

choices.text: Raise every AP's power for the season
choices.why: The scanners' weak transmitters still limit the uplink, and overlap grows.

choices.text: Measure it as it is now
choices.why: Right. The stock is part of the building, and March measured a different one.

choices.text: Trust the March document, since it passed
choices.why: It describes the building on the day it was walked, and that building had empty racks.

choices.text: Replace the scanners with laptops
choices.why: The requirement is the scanners; the design has to serve them.

prompt: In free space, every doubling of the distance adds ___ dB of path loss.
